title: Uveal Emergencies: VKH Disease & Sympathetic Ophthalmia
summary: An exhaustive clinical guide to Vogt–Koyanagi–Harada disease and Sympathetic Ophthalmia—two profound multisystem inflammatory conditions characterized by bilateral granulomatous panuveitis and autoimmune-mediated melanocyte targeting.

branches: Multisystem inflammatory disease: Affects eyes (bilateral granulomatous panuveitis), ears, brain, skin, and hair.
Mechanism: T-cell-mediated autoimmune disease directed against melanocyte antigen(s).
Risk Factors: Higher prevalence in darker-skinned races (Asians, Native Americans, Hispanics, Middle and Far East).
Demographics: Commonest in women in their 3rd and 4th decades; can occur in either sex at any age.
Genetic Association: HLA-DR4, notably HLA-DRB1*0405 (recognizes various melanocyte proteins).
Triggers: May arise after cutaneous injury, presumably via liberation of melanocyte antigens.

sections.title: Clinical Features: Systemic & Prodrome
content: Prodrome: Fever, meningism, and auditory symptoms for a few days before blurring/profound visual loss.
Neurological: Sterile meningitis (headache, neck stiffness), encephalitis (convulsions, altered consciousness), cranial neuropathies (including ocular motility disturbance).
Auditory: Tinnitus, deafness, vertigo.
Cutaneous (Late features): Vitiligo, alopecia, poliosis.

sections.title: Clinical Features: Ophthalmic & Complications
content: Anterior Uveitis: Bilateral granulomatous anterior uveitis, PS (Posterior Synechiae), iris nodules, AC (Anterior Chamber) shallowing.

Posterior Uveitis: Multifocal choroiditis, multifocal detachments of sensory retina, ERD (Exudative Retinal Detachment), choroidal depigmentation ('sunset glow fundus'), Dalen–Fuchs’ nodules (peripheral yellow-white choroidal granulomas), subretinal fibrosis.
Complications: Cataract, glaucoma, CNV (Choroidal Neovascular) membrane.

sections.title: VKH Investigations
content: OCT: Used to monitor extent and height of serous detachments.
FFA: Focal areas of delay in choroidal perfusion, multifocal areas of pinpoint leakage, large placoid areas of hyperfluorescence, pooling within subretinal fluid (SRF), and optic nerve staining.
US: Low to medium reflective diffuse choroidal thickening.
LP (Not always required): Lymphocytic pleocytosis.

sections.title: Management of VKH
content: Step 1: Liaise with physician.
Step 2: Start high-dose systemic corticosteroids (e.g. 1–2mg/kg/d prednisolone PO or IVMP 1g/d for 3d).
Step 3: For resistant or recurrent disease, add corticosteroid-sparing agents (immunosuppressants).
Immunosuppressants include: Methotrexate, azathioprine, mycophenolate mofetil, tacrolimus, and ciclosporin.

sections.title: Table 11.15: Revised Diagnostic Criteria for VKH (AUS Criteria)

rows: No history of penetrating ocular trauma or surgery preceding initial onset of uveitis.
No clinical or laboratory evidence suggestive of other ocular disease entities.
(1) Diffuse choroiditis (focal SRF or bullous serous retinal detachments). (2) If equivocal: Characteristic FFA findings AND diffuse choroidal thickening (no posterior scleritis on US).

(1) History of early features AND (2) Two or more of: Ocular depigmentation (sunset glow fundus or Sugiura sign), Nummular chorioretinal depigmented scars, RPE clumping/migration, Recurrent or chronic anterior uveitis.
(a) Meningismus (malaise, fever, headache, nausea, abdominal pain, neck/back stiffness), (b) Tinnitus, (c) CSF pleocytosis.
Findings not preceding ocular/CNS disease: (a) Alopecia, (b) Poliosis, (c) Vitiligo.

branches: Definition: Rare bilateral granulomatous panuveitis with remarkable parallels to VKH.
Causality: Related to antecedent trauma or surgery.
Timing: Can occur within a few days or over 60y later; usually arises between 1 and 12mo after injury.
Pathogenesis: T-cell-mediated response to ocular antigen liberated during initial insult.
BOSU Study findings: Commonest cause was ocular (vitreoretinal) surgery.

sections.title: Verbatim Statistics & Risk
sections.content: It occurs in 0.1% of cases of penetrating ocular trauma and in 0.01% of cases of routine vitrectomy. In one prospective study (BOSU), the commonest cause of sympathetic ophthalmia was ocular (particularly vitreoretinal) surgery.

sections.title: SO Clinical Features
content: Anterior: Bilateral granulomatous anterior uveitis with mutton fat KPs, PS.
Posterior: Vitritis, choroidal infiltration, Dalen–Fuchs nodules, macular oedema, ERD; the exciting eye may be phthsical.
Complications: Cataract, 2° glaucoma, end-stage disease (optic atrophy, chorioretinal scarring).
Systemic: As for VKH, but systemic involvement less common.

sections.title: SO Prevention: The Window of Opportunity
content: 7-10 Days: Short window after trauma where enucleation almost certainly prevents sympathetic ophthalmia.
Patient Selection: Best option for blind, painful eyes with no hope of useful vision.
Modern Trend: Preserve the eye where possible for many traumatized eyes with visual potential.

sections.title: SO Treatment & Prognosis
content: Enucleation role: Controversial once inflammation develops; may modify disease if performed within 2wk of symptoms.
Immunosuppression: Start high-dose systemic corticosteroids (1–2mg/kg/d prednisolone PO or IVMP 1g/d for 3d).
Corticosteroid-sparing agents: Consider Methotrexate, azathioprine, ciclosporin, mycophenolate mofetil, and tacrolimus for resistant/recurrent disease or side effects.
Outcome: With aggressive treatment, around 60% may achieve >6/15 in the sympathizing eye.
